items.followUp: State two functions of bile in digestion.

rubric.why: Bile salts break large fat globules into smaller droplets, increasing the surface area for lipase.
rubric.description: Bile emulsifies fats.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that bile emulsifies fats or breaks fat into small droplets.

rubric.why: Bile helps neutralize acidic food coming from the stomach and makes the small intestine suitable for digestive enzymes.
rubric.description: Bile neutralizes acidic chyme and provides an alkaline medium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that bile neutralizes stomach acid or provides an alkaline medium.

modelAnswer: Bile is produced by the liver and stored in the gall bladder.
Bile salts emulsify fats into small droplets, increasing the surface area for lipase.
Bile also neutralizes acidic chyme from the stomach and provides an alkaline medium in the small intestine.

items.followUp: Explain how cohesion and transpiration help water rise in a plant.

rubric.why: Evaporation of water from leaf surfaces creates tension that pulls water upward through the plant.
rubric.description: Transpiration from leaves creates the pulling force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying water loss or evaporation from leaves as the cause of the pull.

rubric.why: Cohesion keeps water molecules joined in a continuous column, allowing the pull to be transmitted down the xylem.
rubric.description: Cohesion maintains a continuous column of water in the xylem.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining cohesion or the continuous water column.

modelAnswer: Water evaporates from the surfaces of leaf cells and leaves through the stomata; this transpiration creates tension or a pulling force.
Cohesion between water molecules keeps them joined in a continuous column in the xylem, so the pull draws water upward from the roots.

items.followUp: Define tissue and give one example of a tissue forming an organ.

rubric.why: An organ is made from different tissues working together to perform a particular function.
rubric.description: Defines the organ level and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that an organ consists of different tissues working together; award 1 mark for a correct example such as the stomach or heart.

rubric.why: An organ system consists of organs working together to carry out a major body function.
rubric.description: Defines the organ-system level and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that an organ system consists of organs working together; award 1 mark for a correct example such as the digestive system or circulatory system.

modelAnswer: At the organ level, different tissues are organized and work together to perform a specific function; for example, the stomach is an organ.
At the organ-system level, different organs work together to perform a major function; for example, the stomach, intestines and other organs form the digestive system.

items.followUp: Describe the structure and two functions of the nucleus.

rubric.why: The nucleus acts as the cell's control centre.
rubric.description: States a function of the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the nucleus controls cell activities.

rubric.why: The nucleus contains the cell's genetic material, which is organized into chromosomes.
rubric.description: States that the nucleus contains hereditary material.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying hereditary information, genetic material or chromosomes in the nucleus.

rubric.why: The nuclear envelope surrounds the nucleus and has pores.
rubric.description: Describes the nuclear envelope.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the nuclear membrane or envelope as a surrounding structure.

rubric.why: A correct diagram should show the main internal structures of the nucleus, clearly labelled.
rubric.description: Draws and labels a nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a recognizable nucleus with an envelope and at least two correct internal labels; award 1 mark for clear, correct labels including the nucleolus and chromatin or nucleoplasm.

modelAnswer: The nucleus controls the activities of the cell and contains hereditary information in the form of chromosomes.
It is surrounded by a double nuclear membrane with pores; its interior contains nucleoplasm, chromatin and a nucleolus.
Diagram construction: Draw a circle about 6 cm in diameter for the nucleus; draw a second, closely spaced circle inside it to show the double nuclear membrane.
Add several small openings across the two circles to represent nuclear pores; draw thread-like chromatin and one small circle for the nucleolus inside the nucleus.
Label the diagram: nuclear membrane, nuclear pore, nucleoplasm, chromatin and nucleolus.

items.followUp: Name the three main groups of organisms in Kingdom Protista and give one example of each.

rubric.why: Protozoans are animal-like protists; Amoeba is a suitable example.
rubric.description: Explains animal-like protists and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying protozoans or animal-like protists and 1 mark for a correct example, such as Amoeba or Paramecium.

rubric.why: Algae are plant-like protists; examples include Euglena and diatoms.
rubric.description: Identifies plant-like protists and an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying algae or plant-like protists, with a suitable example.

rubric.why: Slime molds and water molds are fungus-like protists.
rubric.description: Identifies fungus-like protists.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying slime molds, water molds or fungus-like protists.

modelAnswer: The three main types of organisms in Kingdom Protista are protozoans, algae and fungus-like protists.
Protozoans are animal-like and usually move to obtain food; examples include Amoeba and Paramecium.
Algae are plant-like and make food by photosynthesis; examples include Euglena and diatoms.
Fungus-like protists include slime molds and water molds; they commonly obtain food from organic matter.

items.followUp: Explain how carbon dioxide is converted into carbohydrate during the Calvin cycle.

rubric.why: The reactions occur in the chloroplast stroma and do not use light directly.
rubric.description: Gives the location and light requirement of the dark reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the stroma or stating that the reaction does not directly require light.

rubric.why: Carbon dioxide is fixed by combining with RuBP, forming PGA.
rubric.description: Describes carbon fixation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that carbon dioxide is fixed to RuBP and forms PGA.

rubric.why: ATP and NADPH from the light reaction provide energy and reducing power to convert PGA into PGAL.
rubric.description: Describes the reduction of PGA to PGAL using products of the light reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming ATP and NADPH as inputs; award 1 mark for stating that they help convert PGA into PGAL.

rubric.why: Some PGAL is used to make carbohydrate, while the remainder regenerates RuBP so the cycle can continue.
rubric.description: States the products and regeneration step.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that PGAL forms carbohydrate and/or that RuBP is regenerated.

modelAnswer: The dark reaction, or Calvin cycle, occurs in the stroma of the chloroplast and does not require light directly.
Carbon dioxide combines with RuBP, forming PGA; this step is called carbon fixation.
ATP and NADPH made during the light reaction provide energy and hydrogen to convert PGA into PGAL.
Some PGAL is used to make glucose and other carbohydrates.
The remaining PGAL regenerates RuBP, allowing the cycle to continue.

items.followUp: Describe how proteins and fats are digested in the small intestine.

rubric.why: Bile neutralizes acidic chyme and emulsifies fats in the small intestine.
rubric.description: Explains the role of bile.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that bile neutralizes acid or emulsifies fats.

rubric.why: Pancreatic juice contains enzymes that digest carbohydrates, proteins and fats.
rubric.description: Identifies pancreatic juice and its digestive enzymes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming pancreatic juice and at least one appropriate enzyme or describing its role.

rubric.why: Intestinal enzymes complete digestion, producing absorbable small molecules.
rubric.description: Gives the final products of digestion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly matching digested food to products, such as proteins to amino acids or fats to fatty acids and glycerol.

rubric.why: The small intestine absorbs the products of digestion through villi.
rubric.description: Explains absorption in the small intestine.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that digested nutrients are absorbed through villi into blood or lymph.

modelAnswer: In the small intestine, bile from the liver neutralizes acidic chyme and emulsifies fats into small droplets.
Pancreatic juice enters the small intestine: amylase digests starch, trypsin digests proteins, and lipase digests fats.
Intestinal juice completes digestion: carbohydrates become glucose, proteins become amino acids, and fats become fatty acids and glycerol.
The digested nutrients are absorbed through the villi of the small intestine into the blood or lymph.

items.followUp: What is an organism's habitat? Give one example.

rubric.why: A habitat is the place or environment where an organism lives.
rubric.description: Defines habitat.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining a habitat as the place or environment where an organism lives.

rubric.why: A suitable example shows understanding that habitats are places with conditions that support organisms.
rubric.description: Gives an example of a habitat.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct habitat example, such as a pond, forest, desert or ocean.

modelAnswer: A habitat is the natural place or environment where an organism lives.
For example, a pond is a habitat for many aquatic organisms.
